passage: Last December I told everyone the chemistry syllabus was easy. I'm Vaibhav, and I'd read the textbook once and every page looked familiar. Reactions, formulas, diagrams: I nodded at all of them. My sister Yamini kept writing answers from memory on a whiteboard, and I laughed at her. "Why practise what you already know?" Then the prelim paper asked me to write the full equation for an experiment. I stared at the blank line. I could picture the page, even the colour of the heading, but nothing came out. I got 41. The page had felt known because I'd seen it, not because I could produce it. Yamini got 88. She didn't say a word, which was worse.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav score in the chemistry prelim?
qa.a: Vaibhav got 41.

qa.q: Why did the syllabus feel easy to Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt confident because every page looked familiar after one reading, and that recognition felt like knowing. Vaibhav never tested whether the answers could be written from memory.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav borrow from Yamini's method?
qa.a: Close the book and write answers from memory, like Yamini on the whiteboard; whatever can't be recalled shows exactly what still needs revising.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt when Vaibhav laughed at her whiteboard practice?
qa.a: Yamini may have felt a little hurt or annoyed but kept to her method, and her 88 later showed that recalling from memory was worth the effort.

grounding: Shows a teenager who found the syllabus easy because it looked familiar, skipped recall practice and could not produce the answers in the exam.

passage:
Tuition centre note, Class 10 maths. Vikas sir, Saturday.
Observation: On Monday Deepak told me he would skip the revision worksheet because "trigonometry is easy, I know all of it." When I explained a solved example, he nodded along: "Yes, yes, I've seen this." In Thursday's closed-book test he left four of six questions blank. Afterwards he said, "But I knew all this when I read it!" He seemed genuinely surprised, not lazy.
What I did next: I gave him three fresh questions and asked him to solve them without looking, then check against the book. He got one right. We agreed he will do this "blank page test" before calling any chapter done.

qa.q: How many of the six questions did Deepak leave blank?
qa.a: Deepak left four of six questions blank.

qa.q: Why was Deepak genuinely surprised by the test?
qa.a: When he read the chapter the examples looked familiar, and that ease felt like knowing; he had never tried to produce the answers alone.

qa.q: Why is the blank page test a good fix for Deepak?
qa.a: Solving without looking shows what he can actually recall, so his confidence gets checked against real output before he calls a chapter done.

qa.q: How does Vikas sir read Deepak's behaviour?
qa.a: Vikas sir sees honest overconfidence rather than laziness, which is why the response is a practical test and not a scolding.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy who calls a chapter easy because it looks familiar and skips revision, then cannot recall it in a test.

passage:
Saturday night
Signed up to play guitar at the annual day. Solo! Ma'am asked if I was sure, since I've had only two lessons with Shreya didi, and I said yes, obviously. I've watched something like a hundred videos of that song. I know exactly how it goes. Manjula from my class said she'd sing along. Tonight I played the full song for Amma. My fingers kept landing on the wrong strings, the chord change in the chorus sounded like a cat on a tin roof, and I stopped three times. Amma clapped anyway and called me her rockstar son. Still, the function is in nine days. I can hear it perfectly in my head. Why can't my hands do it?
Mridul

qa.q: How many guitar lessons has Mridul had?
qa.a: Mridul has had only two lessons with Shreya didi.

qa.q: Why did Mridul feel sure enough to sign up for a solo?
qa.a: He felt confident because he had watched about a hundred videos of the song and could hear it perfectly in his head. Knowing how it sounds felt like being able to play it.

qa.q: What small step would help Mridul before the annual day?
qa.a: He could play the song daily for someone and count the stops, ask Shreya didi which part to simplify, and decide honestly whether a shorter piece is wiser. 🙂

qa.q: How might Manjula feel about singing along on the day?
qa.a: Manjula may feel nervous, since her part depends on his playing and she has no idea he struggles with the chorus.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy rating his guitar skill high after two lessons because the song feels familiar, then finding he cannot play it.

qa.q: Why does Mihir feel he knows the chapter?

passage: On his uncle's farm outside Sangli, Ganesh, sixteen, had driven the tractor twice, both times with his aunt Vasudha beside him on the flat stretch near the shed. On the third morning he told his cousin Pooja, "I've got it. I'll take it to the far field myself." "Alone? Aai said—" "It's simple. Clutch, gear, go. I've done it twice." Vasudha came out of the kitchen wiping her hands. "Ganesh, tell me how you'd go down the slope by the canal." He shrugged. "Same as on the flat." Vasudha shook her head. "That's the part you haven't done. On a slope you need a low gear before you start down." Ganesh went red. He hadn't known that at all. Two tries on flat ground had felt like knowing everything. "Okay," he said. "Will you sit with me on the slope?" Pooja grinned. "I'm coming too."

qa.q: How many times had Ganesh driven the tractor?
qa.a: He had driven the tractor twice.

qa.q: Why did Ganesh think driving to the far field alone would be simple?
qa.a: Two easy tries on flat ground felt like he had mastered it. He didn't know enough yet to realise the slope was a different skill.

qa.q: Which question from Vasudha was the turning point, and why?
qa.a: Asking how he would go down the slope by the canal. His answer showed him, not her, the gap in what he knew, so he asked her to sit with him.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when Ganesh announced he'd go alone?
qa.a: Pooja seemed uneasy, starting to remind him what Aai said, and then relieved and cheerful once he agreed to have Vasudha along.

grounding: A teenage boy thinks he can drive a tractor alone after two tries, until his aunt asks him about a part he has never done.
